details:
**Contendings with Set**
Horus, son of Isis and Osiris, fought his uncle Set (Seth), who had murdered and dismembered Osiris, for the throne of Egypt. The Contendings of Horus and Seth describe a dispute that dragged on for eighty years before the Ennead, the council of gods, ruled in Horus's favor and made him king. Set was sent off to rule the deserts and storms.

**The stone boat race**
In one of the contests, Horus and Set agreed to race in boats made of stone. Horus secretly built his boat out of wood (cedar) and plastered or painted it gray so that it looked like stone, while Set built a real stone boat, which sank. This is the most frequently mentioned contest.

**Wedjat (Eye of Horus)**
During their fighting, Set gouged out Horus's eye (or both eyes). The wedjat (also spelled wadjet or udjat) eye became a protective amulet representing healing and wholeness. Horus's right eye was associated with the sun and his left, damaged eye with the moon, which explains why the moon is dimmer than the sun. The parts of the eye symbol were also used to write fractions from one half to one sixty-fourth.

**Hathor heals his eyes with milk**
After Set tore out Horus's eyes and buried them on a mountainside, where they grew into lotus flowers, the goddess Hathor restored his sight by pouring gazelle milk into the empty sockets. Hathor is also usually named as Horus's wife, and in a yearly festival her statue traveled from her temple at Dendera to his at Edfu to reunite the couple.

**Four Sons of Horus and the canopic jars**
Horus's four sons, Imsety (human-headed), Hapi (baboon-headed), Duamutef (jackal-headed), and Qebehsenuef (falcon-headed), each guarded one cardinal direction and one of the organs removed during mummification. Their heads appear on the lids of the four canopic jars that held those organs.

**Falcon-headed sky god and the pharaohs**
Horus is usually shown as a falcon or a man with a falcon's head, often wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Each living pharaoh was considered an earthly embodiment of Horus, while a dead king became identified with Osiris.

**Harpocrates and the finger to the lips**
Horus the Child (Har-pa-khered) was shown as a naked boy with the sidelock of youth and a finger to his lips. The Greeks and Romans misunderstood the gesture as a call for silence and worshipped him as Harpocrates, god of silence and secrets; he was linked to the phrase "sub rosa." Aleister Crowley's religion Thelema says the world is now in the "Aeon of Horus."

**Sobek retrieves his severed hands**
After Horus's semen was involved in a contest with Set, Isis cut off his hands, which she considered polluted, and threw them into the marshes or the Nile, then made him new ones. The crocodile god Sobek fished the original hands out of the water with a fish trap.

**The contaminated lettuce**
When Set tried to seduce or rape Horus to show his dominance over him, Horus caught Set's semen in his hand. Isis then had Horus put his own semen on the lettuce in Set's garden, which Set ate. When the gods called out to each spirit, Set's semen answered from the marshes, while Horus's answered from inside Set, proving to the Ennead that Horus had dominated him.

**The hippopotamus contest and Isis's beheading**
Horus and Set changed into hippopotamuses and competed to see who could stay underwater longer. Isis threw a copper harpoon to help her son, but she first struck Horus by mistake, and when she then hit Set, she released him out of pity because he was her brother. In a rage, Horus cut off his mother's head, which the gods later restored, sometimes as a cow's head.

**Set's lost testicles**
In the battle in which Horus lost his eye, he tore off one of Set's testicles (or both). This was said to explain why Set's domain, the desert, is infertile.

**Conception and birth on Chemmis**
Isis conceived Horus by reassembling and briefly reviving the dead Osiris, making a replacement for his missing phallus. She then hid the infant Horus from Set in the papyrus marshes on the island of Chemmis in the Nile Delta, where he was raised with the help of the cobra goddess Wadjet (called Buto by the Greeks).

**Nekhen (Hierakonpolis) and Edfu**
Nekhen in Upper Egypt was the oldest center of Horus worship; the Greeks called it Hierakonpolis, "City of the Hawk." The Ptolemaic Temple of Edfu, one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, was also dedicated to him and held an annual Festival of Victory celebrating his defeat of Set.

**Forms: Horus the Elder, Behdety, and Ra-Horakhty**
Horus appears in many forms. Horus the Elder (Haroeris, Heru-ur) was an older form linked to Nekhen. Horus of Behdet (Behdety) was shown as the winged sun disk, and Horakhty ("Horus of the Two Horizons") was merged with Ra as Ra-Horakhty, the rising and setting sun. As Mekhenty-er-irty, a form of him without eyes, he was linked to the blind and to nights with no moon.
